You've now seen the big picture of how to evaluate
and improve an agent.

Before you put that process into practice, you need a way to see what
the agent actually does as it works through a task.

That's because if you only look at the agent's input and output,
you miss what it does in between.

For example, a customer might ask Northwind whether a jacket is
available in their size, and the agent says yes.

But between that question and the answer, the agent may be calling
tools to look up the jacket and check inventory,
interpreting the results, and deciding what to do next as it goes.
Problems can occur at any of those steps.

For example, the agent might have skipped the inventory check
and simply made up the answer that the jacket was in stock.

From the response alone, you wouldn't know whether the agent had
actually checked the inventory.

So before you get into evaluations, you need a window into agent
behavior. That's what a trace provides.

So in this video, you'll see how traces are put together,
what their different parts record,
and how you can use them to investigate the agent's behavior.
A trace brings together the recorded steps from one run of your agent.

A run is a single execution of the agent, from receiving a request to
finishing its response.

To see how that works, imagine a Northwind customer
asking for a refund.

The agent might look up their order, check the return policy,
and request the refund.

A trace records the model calls and tool calls along the way.
Each recorded operation is called a span, with a beginning and an end.

So the order lookup could be one span,
and processing the refund could be another.

Larger operations can contain smaller operations,
with their spans nested inside. That gives you a tree of spans.

The root span covers the whole request, with child spans beneath it
for operations such as the order lookup and refund.

The root is their parent, and those child spans can have
children of their own.

The tree shows what happened during the run,
based on the operations your application records.

It isn't a fixed plan for the agent to follow,
so another run might include different tool calls or repeated steps.

Now that you've seen how spans fit together,
let's look at what each span records about an operation.

Take the span for looking up the customer's order. Its name tells you
which operation ran, and its type identifies it as a tool call.

The recorded input shows what was sent to the tool,
such as an order ID.

The output shows what came back, such as the order details
and the purchase price.

If the agent refunds the wrong amount, you can check whether it looked
up the right order and what purchase price the tool returned.
A model-call span gives you a different view.

Its input can include the customer's message,
the agent's instructions, and information returned by earlier tools.

Its output records what the model generated,
that might be an answer for the customer or a request to use a tool.

For model calls, you can also capture token usage,
a measure of how much text the model took in and generated,
along with the model version and the prompt used.
These details can be recorded as attributes on the span.

They help you understand the conditions of each run and check what
changed when comparing results.

Together, the model-call and tool-call spans let you follow
which tools the model called, what they returned,
and how the model responded afterward.

Spans also record when each operation started and ended,
so you can see how long it took.

If the customer waited a long time, you can check whether the delay
came from the model call or the order lookup.

You can also spot repeated tool calls that added unnecessary work,
even if the agent eventually gave a correct answer.

Just remember, a trace doesn't show everything
happening inside the model.

Even any reasoning text it includes is generated output,
not a direct view of the model's internal workings.

So how do you get your application to record these traces? You add
code that captures information about the operations as they happen.

Adding that recording is called instrumentation.
You don't necessarily have to write all that code yourself.

Depending on the framework and tracing integration,
you can automatically capture model calls and tool calls,
including their inputs, outputs, and timing.

You can also add recording around your own functions when you need to
capture something the integration doesn't cover.

In this course, you'll use Phoenix to collect and inspect the traces.
The tracing integration sends it the recorded spans.

You can then open a run, follow the tree, and select a span to inspect
its recorded inputs, outputs, and other details.

The lab takes you through setting up that connection.
The concepts aren't specific to Phoenix though.

You can use other tracing tools or write your own code to record
and inspect the same information.

The important limit is that a trace only contains what
your setup recorded.

If an order lookup wasn't instrumented, you might see the model calls,
but miss the lookup between them.

So an absent span doesn't automatically mean the
agent skipped an action.

Before drawing that conclusion, you need to know that the relevant
work was being captured.

With those records in place, now suppose a refund for a
customer goes wrong.

The agent tells the customer their refund was processed, but the trace
shows that the refund tool reported it hadn't been completed.

The model got that failure message, but still told the customer the
refund was on its way.
The trace gives you evidence you can use to evaluate the agent.

You can evaluate one operation, such as whether the agent looked up
the right order, or the overall result,
such as whether it handled the refund correctly.

Once you've evaluated it, you can record your assessment
alongside the trace.

In Phoenix, that's called an annotation, which can include a label
or a score and an explanation.

Also note that a conversation between a customer and the agent can
include several runs.

For example, the agent handles a refund request and responds,
then handles the customer's follow-up question in another run.

Each run has its own trace, which can contain multiple model
calls and tool calls.

A shared session ID groups those traces so you can follow the whole
conversation. That wraps up module one.

You've seen why evals matter, how the evaluation process fits
together, and how traces let you see what an agent actually did.

You'll get more practice working with traces in the lab
and graded assignment.

Then, in module two, you'll start putting that evaluation
process into practice,

working out what the agent needs to do and investigating
where it falls short.
